notes: Complete EWCA Crim judgment on jury directions in two-party conspiracy cases.

enrichment.short_title: Two-party conspiracy appeal: differing verdicts wrongly permitted where evidence against both defendants was the same
key_facts: Testouri and council housing officer Gordon were tried for conspiracy to defraud Lambeth over inflated decorating/repair invoices on council properties.
The trial judge directed the jury that they could convict Testouri and acquit Gordon because their roles and dishonest intent differed.
The jury convicted Testouri but acquitted Gordon; Testouri appealed against conviction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the Single Judge in the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division).
enrichment.ratio: In a two-defendant conspiracy to defraud, the judge must first ask whether there is evidence of agreement and then whether there is evidence admissible only against one defendant that could be critical; where there is no such unequal evidence and the same evidence is equally admissible against both, the jury must be directed to return the same verdict for each defendant, and a conviction of one with acquittal of the other is inconsistent.
legal_issues: Whether a jury may return different verdicts on a two-party conspiracy count
When a judge must direct 'both guilty or both not guilty' in conspiracy cases
Application of R v Longman, R v Roberts and R v Ashton to differing-verdict directions

notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment refusing anti-suit injunction in parallel English/New York swap litigation.

enrichment.short_title: RBC anti-suit injunction refused where Rabobank pursued parallel New York proceedings under non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause
key_facts: Royal Bank of Canada and Rabobank disputed liability under a Total Return Swap forming part of an Enron-related structured finance transaction governed by an English-law ISDA Master Agreement with a non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause.
Parallel proceedings were brought in England and New York over the same issues; New York trial was listed for January 2004 and the English trial for March 2004.
RBC sought an injunction restraining Rabobank from obtaining any determination in New York save for completing factual discovery.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for an anti-suit injunction in the Commercial Court during concurrent English and New York litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Rabobank not restrained from pursuing New York proceedings to determination.
enrichment.ratio: Concurrent litigation in two jurisdictions does not of itself make foreign proceedings vexatious or oppressive; a non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause may lighten the burden of showing oppressive conduct but does not convert England into an exclusive forum or deprive a party of a legitimate juridical advantage in litigating elsewhere, and it would not be just under section 37 to restrain Rabobank from pursuing duly commenced New York proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether pursuit of parallel New York proceedings was vexatious or oppressive
Effect of a non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause in an ISDA agreement
Whether England was the natural or primary forum
Appropriate use of anti-suit injunctions where foreign courts have accepted jurisdiction

notes: Complete Munby J judgment on media injunction variation and Article 8/10 balancing for competent teenager.

enrichment.short_title: Teenage mother permitted to tell care-system story while anonymity of child X and adopted daughter Y preserved
key_facts: Angela Roddy became pregnant at 12; care and adoption proceedings followed, with long-standing injunctions protecting the identities of Angela, the putative father X, and her daughter Y.
Associated Newspapers applied to vary the injunction so Angela, then nearly 17, could tell her story in the Mail on Sunday without identifying X or Y.
Torbay Borough Council sought wider protection, including to block publication of Angela's story on the ground it might destabilise Y's adoptive placement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to vary or discharge contra mundum publication injunctions in the Family Division.
enrichment.outcome: Original injunction discharged; Angela permitted to publish with her consent; injunctions preserving anonymity of X and Y maintained; council's attempt to restrain publication of Angela's story rejected.
enrichment.ratio: After Re S, the court must conduct an independent Article 8 and Article 10 balancing exercise; a competent 16- or 17-year-old may decide whether to waive privacy and tell her own story, but third-party Article 8 rights justify anonymity orders for X and Y, and under section 12(3) the local authority failed to show a real prospect that wider restraints on Angela's publication were justified.
legal_issues: Whether a competent teenager may exercise Article 8 and Article 10 rights to publish her own story
Balancing media freedom against anonymity of X and Y
Application of section 12(3) Human Rights Act 1998 to interlocutory injunctions
Extent of the court's inherent jurisdiction after Re S

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment quashing prison death inquest for defective neglect directions.

enrichment.short_title: Prison inquest quashed where coroner failed to leave systemic neglect and nurse's gross failure to jury
key_facts: Darren Davies, aged 23, died in HMP Winson Green from cardiac arrest following dehydration and repeated vomiting during heroin withdrawal shortly after reception.
He missed detox medication after a wing move, received inadequate nursing and officer responses over the weekend, and was not referred to a doctor despite worsening symptoms.
After a five-day inquest the jury returned accidental death; the coroner excluded parts of Dr Ralli's evidence and gave confused directions on neglect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by judicial review claimant (deceased's mother) against Moses J's refusal to quash the inquest and order a fresh hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; inquisition quashed; fresh inquest ordered focused on whether systemic neglect contributed to death.
enrichment.ratio: Where a death in custody must be investigated through the inquest as the state's Article 2 procedural vehicle, the jury must be left to consider systemic neglect as well as individual gross failure to provide basic medical attention; a Rule 43 letter is not an adequate substitute for a public neglect verdict, and misdirection excluding that issue renders the inquest inadequate.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'neglect' at an inquest after Jamieson and Middleton
Whether Nurse Spencer's clinical judgment could amount to gross failure
Whether systemic defects in prison healthcare should have been left to the jury
Whether a fresh inquest was necessary despite extensive earlier evidence

notes: Complete appeal by case stated on PACE Code D identification evidence and reporting restrictions.

enrichment.short_title: Youth court convictions upheld despite failure to hold identification parade for sole recognition witness
key_facts: Three young defendants were convicted after a street disturbance in Havant in which witness A was attacked and suffered a double arm fracture.
The sole identifying witness, 14-year-old B, knew the appellants well; no video identification procedure was held before trial despite a conceded breach of PACE Code D.
The district judge admitted B's recognition evidence, rejected no-case submissions, and convicted on violent disorder and wounding counts while acquitting on some charges and co-defendant H.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from South and South East Hampshire Youth Court to the Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; case stated questions answered 'yes'; statutory reporting restrictions left in place for the appeal hearing.
enrichment.ratio: A breach of PACE Code D does not automatically exclude identification evidence; where a witness knew the defendants well and gave sustained recognition evidence, the youth court could properly exercise its section 78 discretion to admit the evidence and convict, and selective acquittals on some counts did not render the remaining convictions irrational.
legal_issues: Admissibility of identification evidence despite Code D breach
Exercise of section 78 discretion in recognition cases
Whether no case to answer should have been upheld
Whether inconsistent verdicts between co-defendants vitiated convictions
Reporting restrictions under section 49 on appeal

notes: Complete admin judgment on NASS dispersal and specialist PTSD treatment availability.

enrichment.short_title: NASS Swansea dispersal lawful initially but further medical reconsideration required after new PTSD evidence
key_facts: Ms Wanjugu, a Kenyan asylum seeker with complex chronic PTSD, was receiving specialist treatment from Dr Robertson at the Traumatic Stress Clinic in London.
NASS dispersed her to Swansea in May 2003 despite medical representations that suitable specialist trauma services were unavailable there.
Further psychiatric reports in August and November 2003 indicated deterioration and urgent need for local psychological support.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of NASS dispersal and subsequent refusal to return the claimant to London.
enrichment.outcome: Original May dispersal upheld; maintenance of Swansea placement after later evidence not adequately reasoned; no formal quashing order but NASS undertook to reconsider all medical material within 14 days; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: NASS may disperse asylum seekers outside London as a general policy and is not obliged to treat Traumatic Stress Clinic patients like Medical Foundation torture victims, but once detailed medical evidence showed specialist PTSD services were unavailable in the dispersal area, a decision to maintain that placement required clear medical reasoning and fresh reconsideration of later reports.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of NASS dispersal having regard to medical needs
Whether Medical Foundation exception must be extended to Traumatic Stress Clinic patients
Rationality of maintaining Swansea placement after Dr Robertson's August letter
Appropriate relief where Newcastle offer remained open

notes: Complete TCC preliminary issues appeal on partial incorporation of FIDIC limitation terms.

enrichment.short_title: FIDIC liability cap incorporated in ground investigation agreement but not in main Sual power station design contract
key_facts: CEPAS/Mirant engaged Ove Arup to design civil works for the Sual coal-fired power station in the Philippines; work began under a May 1995 letter of intent for £3.75m.
Arup proposed a FIDIC Model Services Agreement with a five-year liability period and £4m compensation cap, but the payment schedule was never agreed and no formal design contract was signed.
In March 1996 CEPAS accepted Arup's ground investigation proposal marked 'OK', clause 1 of which incorporated the FIDIC main agreement; boiler foundations later failed in 1997.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendants' appeal against Technology and Construction Court preliminary issue determinations on contract formation and incorporation of FIDIC terms.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on issue 4(d): ground investigation agreement held subject to FIDIC terms; appeal dismissed on issues 2 and 5: main design contract remained on letter of intent without FIDIC caps; formal claim letter sufficient if FIDIC applied.
enrichment.ratio: Acceptance of the ground investigation proposal objectively incorporated Revision B FIDIC terms despite the main design agreement not yet being concluded, but signing that side agreement did not by itself bring the main design contract onto FIDIC terms where an essential payment schedule had never been agreed and parties continued on the letter of intent.
legal_issues: Whether FIDIC five-year limitation and £4m cap applied to the design contract
Construction of clause 1 of the ground investigation proposal
Whether acceptance of ancillary proposals could create the main FIDIC contract by estoppel or conduct
Meaning of 'formally made' claim under FIDIC clause 17

notes: Complete permission-to-appeal decision on Brussels Convention Art 18 and employment tribunal review.

enrichment.short_title: Employer could not avoid merits hearing by staying away: Article 18 posed no real submission-to-jurisdiction risk
key_facts: Mr Turner, Harada's in-house solicitor in Madrid, claimed constructive unfair and wrongful dismissal after being instructed to pursue improper tax litigation against HMRC.

Harada contested jurisdiction, then withdrew from the merits hearing before the Ryan tribunal in May 1999 fearing Article 18 Brussels Convention submission, and later sought review after jurisdiction was finally confirmed in 2001.
The Ansell EAT dismissed the review application as unnecessary and ordered costs of £3,158.50.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against two EAT decisions refusing review and awarding costs.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications dismissed; no permission to appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Under Article 18 as interpreted in Elefanten Schuh and related ECJ authorities, a defendant who has raised jurisdiction at the outset does not submit to jurisdiction by defending on the merits when compelled to participate; Harada therefore had no realistic basis to absent itself from the employment tribunal merits hearing and its later review application was unnecessary and vexatious.
legal_issues: Whether participating in an employment tribunal merits hearing while jurisdiction was under appeal constituted submission under Article 18
Whether Harada had good reason to boycott the Ryan tribunal hearing
Lawfulness of EAT costs order under rule 34
Availability of review after final jurisdiction determination

notes: Complete Brussels II jurisdiction ruling in cross-border child contact/residence dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Spanish jurisdiction over child ceased after final divorce order despite later enforcement and custody applications
key_facts: Following a Spanish divorce in June 2001, the mother was permitted to relocate with Alejandro to England with fortnightly contact to the father in England or Spain.
The father's appeal against the relocation order was dismissed in June 2002, but he continued enforcement applications and later sought custody in Spain.
The mother applied in England to vary contact and for a residence order, arguing Brussels II had transferred jurisdiction once the Spanish judgment became final.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Family Division application to determine jurisdiction as between Spanish and English courts under Brussels II.
enrichment.outcome: English court held it had jurisdiction; Spanish jurisdiction had ceased; monthly travel-to-Spain contact provision suspended pending further hearing; matter listed for directions.
enrichment.ratio: Under Brussels II Article 3(3), jurisdiction conferred on the divorce court for parental responsibility ceases once the matrimonial judgment becomes final, and subsequent applications to enforce contact or change residence do not revive or prolong that jurisdiction; a permanent relocation order is itself a final parental-responsibility judgment.
legal_issues: Construction of Article 3(3) Brussels II and when jurisdiction 'ceases'
Whether post-final enforcement proceedings prevent loss of Spanish jurisdiction
Effect of father's May 2003 custody application

notes: Complete Master of the Rolls appeal on scope of Law Society power to impose RFL conditions.

enrichment.short_title: Law Society could impose conditions only at initial RFL registration, not retrospectively after Mathis investigation
key_facts: Michael Shuman, a Texas attorney registered as a foreign lawyer in England, was associated with solicitor Mathialagan's firm Mathis.
Following a 2002 forensic investigation into high-yield investment scheme transactions, the OSS/Law Society imposed wide practice conditions on Shuman's registration.
Shuman had not renewed his registration but the Society kept it live pending SDT proceedings; he appealed under Schedule 14 paragraph 14.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Master of the Rolls against an Adjudication Panel decision imposing conditions on registered foreign lawyer status.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conditions set aside for want of jurisdiction; costs assessed at £13,000 inclusive of VAT payable in 28 days.
enrichment.ratio: Schedule 14 paragraph 2(3) permits the Law Society to impose conditions only when registration is first made (or on reinstatement/revival under paragraphs 12 and 13), not at any later time during an existing registration, and the express later powers in paragraphs 12–13 indicate paragraph 2(3) was not intended as a general ongoing regulatory power.
legal_issues: Construction of 'Any registration may be made subject to such conditions' in Schedule 14 para 2(3)
Whether conditions could be imposed after OSS investigation without renewal application
Relationship between RFL regime and Solicitors Act conditional certificate powers
Appellate jurisdiction under Schedule 14 paragraph 14
